passages.title: The Room Next to the Canteen
passages.passage:
For most of its history, the library at Tran Phu Secondary School sat on the top floor, at the end of a long corridor, behind a heavy door that was usually closed. It was quiet, it was clean, and it was almost always empty. A survey in 2023 found that fewer than one student in ten had borrowed a book that year.

Last summer, the school tried something different. When the old canteen was rebuilt, the library was moved into the room next to it on the ground floor. The heavy door was replaced with a wide open entrance, and the librarian, Mr Khoa, took down the sign that said "Silence". "A library does not have to be a temple," he explains. "It has to be a place people want to walk into."

The new room is not large, but it is arranged so that it is easy to use. Comics and magazines sit on shelves near the entrance, where students can pick them up while they wait for lunch. Novels and study books are further inside. There are beanbags in one corner, and a long table where students may eat a snack while they read, as long as they wipe it afterwards. Borrowing is done on trust: a student simply writes a name and a title in a notebook by the door.

Some teachers were doubtful. They expected noise, mess and missing books. In fact, the number of books that have not come back is lower than it was before the move, and the noise, Mr Khoa says, is "the good kind". Borrowing has risen to four times last year's level, and the beanbags are so popular that the school has ordered more.

The biggest change, though, may be a small one. Students who once went to the library only when a teacher sent them now go because they walk past it every day, and something in the window catches their eye.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How moving and redesigning a school library changed the way students use it
The rules students must follow in the new school canteen
A survey that compared reading habits at several schools
Why the library at Tran Phu Secondary School was nearly closed
questions.explanation: Every paragraph is about the library: where it used to be, how it was moved and rearranged, and what happened afterwards. The survey and the canteen are details that support this, not the main topic.

questions.q: According to the passage, what did the 2023 survey show?
options: That most students wanted the library moved downstairs
That fewer than ten per cent of students had borrowed a book that year
That students preferred comics to novels
That the library was open for fewer than ten hours a week
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the survey found that fewer than one student in ten had borrowed a book that year. One in ten is ten per cent. The other options are not mentioned as survey results.

questions.q: Where in the new library would a student find a magazine?
options: In the notebook kept by the door
On the long table in the middle of the room
Near the entrance, close to where students wait for lunch
Further inside, next to the study books
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says comics and magazines sit on shelves near the entrance. Novels and study books are the ones kept further inside.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, what does "it" in "as long as they wipe it afterwards" refer to?
options: the notebook by the door
the snack
the corner with the beanbags
the long table
questions.explanation: The sentence describes a long table where students may eat a snack while they read; the thing they must wipe afterwards is that table.

questions.q: The word "doubtful" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to
options: not sure the idea would work
surprised
excited
angry
questions.explanation: The teachers were doubtful because they expected noise, mess and missing books — in other words, they were not sure the plan would succeed. Nothing suggests they were angry or excited.

questions.q: More books have gone missing since the library moved to the ground floor.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the number of books that have not come back is lower than it was before the move, so the statement contradicts the passage.

questions.q: Mr Khoa worked as a librarian at another school before coming to Tran Phu.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage tells us what Mr Khoa did and said at Tran Phu, but says nothing about his earlier career, so there is no way to know.

passages.title: Have You Seen Mochi?
passages.passage:
When Linh came home from school on a Tuesday afternoon, the gate was open and her dog, Mochi, was gone. He was a small brown dog with one white ear, and he had never left the yard before. Her mother had already walked around the block twice. Her little brother, Bao, was crying.

Linh's first idea was to post a photo online, and she did. But her grandmother, who does not use a phone, said something that made her stop. "The people who will find him are the people who live on these streets," she said. "Most of them are not looking at a screen. They are looking at the road."

So that evening, Linh and Bao made a poster. The first version was a mess. Bao wanted to write everything: Mochi's favourite food, the songs he liked, the way he barked at motorbikes. Linh crossed most of it out. "Nobody will stop to read all that," she said. What was left was short. A large photo. The words LOST DOG in thick letters. His name, his colour, the white ear, the street where he lived, and a phone number. At the bottom, Bao insisted on adding one line: "He is scared of thunder. Please be kind."

They printed twenty copies and put them on lampposts, on the gate of the market, and in the window of the shop where their mother bought rice. The shop owner promised to tell every customer.

For two days, nothing happened. Then, on Thursday night, the phone rang. A woman from three streets away had seen the poster in the shop window. A small brown dog with a white ear had been sleeping under her stairs since the storm on Tuesday, too frightened to come out.

Bao says the last line of the poster is what did it. Linh is not so sure, but she has kept one copy in her drawer, just in case.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the passage?
options: To explain how to train a dog to stay in the yard
To tell the story of how a family found their lost dog by making a poster
To argue that posting online is useless when a pet is lost
To describe the storm that hit Linh's town on Tuesday
questions.explanation: The passage follows the family from the moment Mochi disappears to the phone call that brings him back, and the poster is at the centre of the story. Linh did post online too, so the passage does not argue that online posts are useless.

questions.q: Why did the grandmother think a poster would work better than an online post?
options: Because the neighbours were more likely to be looking at the street than at a screen
Because the family could not afford to pay for an online advertisement
Because the police had told her to put up posters
Because she did not know how to use the internet
questions.explanation: In paragraph 2 she says the people who will find Mochi are the ones who live on these streets, and most of them are not looking at a screen. She does not use a phone herself, but that is not the reason she gives.

questions.q: The phrase "a mess" in paragraph 3 means that the first poster was
options: printed in the wrong colour
torn and dirty
too small to read
untidy and badly organised
questions.explanation: The sentences that follow explain the mess: Bao wanted to write everything and Linh had to cross most of it out. The problem was too much information, not damage or size.

questions.q: Why had Mochi most likely stayed under the woman's stairs for two days?
options: Because he did not like Linh's family
Because the woman had locked him in
Because he was frightened by the storm
Because he had hurt his leg
questions.explanation: The poster says Mochi is scared of thunder, and paragraph 5 says he had been under the stairs since the storm on Tuesday, too frightened to come out. The passage does not mention an injury or the woman keeping him.

questions.q: Where did the woman see the poster?
options: On the gate of the market
In the window of a shop
On Linh's online post
On a lamppost near her house
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says she had seen the poster in the shop window. Lampposts and the market gate are other places the posters were put, but not where she saw it.

questions.q: The family printed more than twenty copies of the poster.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says they printed twenty copies — exactly twenty, not more — so the statement is false.

questions.q: The woman who found Mochi had a dog of her own.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage says she lived three streets away and saw the poster, but nothing is said about whether she owned a dog.

passages.title: The Third Jar
passages.passage:
When Minh was twelve, he wanted a second-hand guitar that cost 1,400,000 dong. His parents gave him 20,000 dong every school day for snacks, so if he spent nothing at all, the guitar was fourteen weeks away. He was sure he could do it. He lasted four days.

The problem, he now says, was not that he was greedy. It was that he had no plan. Money that sat in his pocket got spent, because there was always a good reason: a friend's birthday, a hot afternoon, a new flavour of ice cream at the school gate.

His grandmother, who had run a small fruit stall for thirty years, listened to his complaint and gave him three old glass jars. On the first she wrote SPEND, on the second SAVE, and on the third she wrote nothing. Every day, Minh was to put half of his money in the first jar and half in the second, and use only the first for anything he wanted. The third jar, she said, was for money that arrived unexpectedly: a gift from an uncle, a prize, a note found in a coat pocket. That money was never to be touched.

Minh thought the rule about the third jar was strange, but he followed it. The SAVE jar grew slowly, at 50,000 dong a week. What surprised him was the third jar. Lucky money at Tet, a small reward for helping a neighbour move house, a 100,000-dong note from his father for a good report: by the end of the term, it held more than the SAVE jar did.

He bought the guitar in May, seventeen weeks after he started. It took longer than his first plan, but this time it actually happened.

Minh still has the jars, though they are now for bigger things. "The trick," he says, "is not to save more. It is to decide where the money goes before it reaches your pocket."

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How a grandmother ran a fruit stall for thirty years
Why children should not receive lucky money at Tet
How a boy learned to save money using a system of three jars
Why second-hand guitars are cheaper than new ones
questions.explanation: The whole passage follows Minh from his failed first attempt to save, through the three-jar system, to buying the guitar. The fruit stall and Tet money are only details.

questions.q: According to Minh, why did his first attempt to save money fail?
options: Because he was too greedy to stop buying ice cream
Because his parents stopped giving him snack money
Because the guitar became more expensive
Because he had no plan and the money in his pocket got spent
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the problem was not that he was greedy. It was that he had no plan. Option D is the tempting half-truth the passage directly rejects.

questions.q: What was the third jar for?
options: Money that arrived unexpectedly, such as a gift or a prize
The half of his daily money he was allowed to spend
Money to pay his grandmother back
Money for a friend's birthday present
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 explains that the third jar was for money that arrived unexpectedly: a gift from an uncle, a prize, a note found in a coat pocket. The daily money was split between the SPEND and SAVE jars.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, "That money was never to be touched" means the money
options: could be used in an emergency
must not be spent
must be counted every day
should be given to someone else
questions.explanation: "Touched" here means used or spent. The grandmother's rule was that money in the third jar stayed there; the passage gives no exception for emergencies.

questions.q: What does Minh mean by his final comment?
options: The best way to save is to ask your parents for more money
Saving is impossible if your pocket money is small
Deciding in advance where money will go matters more than trying to save a larger amount
Money should never be kept in a pocket because it can be lost
questions.explanation: He says the trick is not to save more but to decide where the money goes before it reaches your pocket — the plan comes first, the amount second.

questions.q: Minh bought the guitar sooner than his original plan had predicted.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: His first plan said the guitar was fourteen weeks away, but he bought it seventeen weeks after he started. It took longer, not less time, so the statement is false.

questions.q: Minh's grandmother had used the three-jar method herself when she ran her stall.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: We are told she ran a fruit stall for thirty years and gave Minh the jars, but the passage never says whether she used the method herself.

passages.title: Lane Six
passages.passage:
The pool at the district sports centre looked much bigger on the morning of the race than it had during training. Perhaps it was the flags, or the rows of parents on the plastic seats, or the loudspeaker that kept calling out names. Whatever it was, Hoang, who was eleven and had been swimming for less than a year, suddenly felt very small.

His event was the 50-metre freestyle, and he had been given lane six, at the edge of the pool. His coach, Ms Yen, said this was good news. "The fast swimmers are in the middle lanes," she said. "Nobody expects anything from lane six. You can just swim." Hoang did not find this as comforting as she meant it to be.

Waiting behind the block was the worst part. He checked his goggles four times. He watched the boy in lane five, who was taller and wore a proper racing cap, shake out his arms like someone on television. When the whistle went, Hoang stepped up onto the block and felt his legs tremble.

Then the horn sounded, and there was no more time to worry. He hit the water badly, too flat, and swallowed a mouthful of it. For the first few strokes he could not see anyone else and thought he must be last. Halfway down the pool, though, he settled into the rhythm he had practised, and stopped thinking about lanes and caps and parents altogether.

He touched the wall fifth out of eight. His time, 41.2 seconds, was two seconds slower than his best in training. The boy in lane five won.

Ms Yen met him with a towel. "Terrible dive," she said. "Good race." Hoang understood the difference. The dive could be fixed in a week. What could not be taught was the moment, halfway down the pool, when he had forgotten to be afraid. He asked her when the next race was.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why the middle lanes of a pool are given to the fastest swimmers
A coach who was disappointed with her swimmer's result
How to perform a perfect racing dive
A boy's first swimming race and what he discovered about himself during it
questions.explanation: The passage follows Hoang from his nerves before the race to the moment he forgot to be afraid and asked about the next one. The lanes and the dive are details, and Ms Yen calls it a good race, so she is not disappointed.

questions.q: Why did Ms Yen say that lane six was good news?
options: Because it was the closest lane to the parents' seats
Because the water was calmer at the edge of the pool
Because nobody would expect anything from a swimmer there, so Hoang could just swim
Because the boy in lane five was slow
questions.explanation: She explains in paragraph 2 that the fast swimmers are in the middle lanes and nobody expects anything from lane six. The boy in lane five, in fact, went on to win.

questions.q: In paragraph 2, what does "this" in "said this was good news" refer to?
options: The loudspeaker calling out names
Hoang being given lane six
The 50-metre freestyle event
The fact that Hoang had trained for less than a year
questions.explanation: The previous sentence says he had been given lane six, at the edge of the pool; "this" points back to that lane assignment, which Ms Yen then explains is a good thing.

questions.q: The word "comforting" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: reassuring
surprising
confusing
funny
questions.explanation: Ms Yen meant her words to make Hoang feel calmer and less worried — to reassure him — but he did not find this as comforting as she meant it to be.

questions.q: Why does Hoang ask about the next race at the end of the passage?
options: Because he thinks he can win if he gets a middle lane
Because he wants to beat the boy in lane five
Because Ms Yen told him he had to enter it
Because he had found a moment during the race when he stopped being afraid, and wants to feel it again
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the thing that could not be taught was the moment when he had forgotten to be afraid, and the very next sentence is his question about the next race. Nothing in the passage mentions revenge on lane five or a middle lane.

questions.q: Hoang swam faster in the race than he ever had in training.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 says his time was two seconds slower than his best in training, so the statement contradicts the passage.

questions.q: The boy in lane five had won races before this one.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: We know he was taller, wore a proper racing cap, and won this race, but the passage says nothing about his earlier results.
